{{Short description|Complex analysis theorem}}
{{distinguish|Casorati&ndash;Sokhotski&ndash;Weierstrass theorem}}{{More footnotes|article|date=September 2019}}
The '''Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem''' (Polish spelling is ''Sochocki'') is a [[theorem]] in [[complex analysis]], which helps in evaluating certain integrals. The real-line version of it ([[#Version for the real line|see below]]) is often used in physics, although rarely referred to by name. The theorem is named after [[Julian Sochocki]], who proved it in 1868, and [[Josip Plemelj]], who rediscovered it as a main ingredient of his solution of the [[Riemann–Hilbert problem]] in 1908.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kress |first1=Rainer |title=Linear Integral Equations |year=2012 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-97146-4 |page=88 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Linear_Integral_Equations/r63rCAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=0 |language=en}}</ref>

== Statement of the theorem ==
Let <math>C</math> be a smooth [[Jordan curve|closed simple curve]] in the plane, and <math>\varphi</math> an [[Holomorphic function|analytic function]] on <math>C</math>. Note that the [[Cauchy's integral formula|Cauchy-type integral]]

:<math> \phi(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_C\frac{\varphi(\zeta) \, d\zeta}{\zeta-z}, </math>

cannot be evaluated for any <math>z</math> on the curve <math>C</math>. However, on the interior and exterior of the curve, the integral produces analytic functions, which will be denoted <math>\phi_i</math> inside <math>C</math> and <math>\phi_e</math> outside. The Sokhotski&ndash;Plemelj formulas relate the limiting boundary values of these two analytic functions at a point <math>z</math> on <math>C</math> and the [[Cauchy principal value]] <math>\mathcal{P}</math> of the integral:

:<math>\lim_{w \to z}\phi_i(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\mathcal{P}\int_C\frac{\varphi(\zeta) \, d\zeta}{\zeta-z} + \frac{1}{2}\varphi(z),</math>

:<math>\lim_{w \to z}\phi_e(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\mathcal{P}\int_C\frac{\varphi(\zeta) \, d\zeta}{\zeta-z}-\frac{1}{2}\varphi(z). </math>

Subsequent generalizations relax the smoothness requirements on curve <math>C</math> and the function <math>\varphi</math>.

==Version for the real line==
{{See also|Kramers–Kronig relations}}
Especially important is the version for integrals over the real line.

:<math> \lim_{\varepsilon\to0^{+}} \frac{1}{x\pm i\varepsilon}= \mp i\pi\delta(x) + {\mathcal{P}} {\Big(\frac{1}{x}\Big)}.</math>

where <math>\delta(x)</math> is the [[Dirac delta function]] where <math>\mathcal{P}</math> denotes the [[Cauchy principal value]]. One may take the difference of these two equalities to obtain

:<math> \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \left[ \frac{1}{x-i\varepsilon} - \frac{1}{x+i\varepsilon} \right] = 2\pi i \delta(x).</math>

These formulae should be interpreted as integral equalities, as follows: Let <math>f</math> be a [[complex number|complex]]-valued function which is defined and continuous on the real line, and let <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> be real constants with <math>a < 0 < b</math>. Then

:<math>\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \int_a^b \frac{f(x)}{x\pm i \varepsilon}\,dx = \mp i \pi f(0) + \mathcal{P}\int_a^b \frac{f(x)}{x}\, dx</math>

and

:<math>\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+ } \int_a^b \left[ \frac{f(x)}{x- i \varepsilon} - \frac{f(x)}{x+ i \varepsilon} \right] \, dx = 2 \pi i f(0)</math>

Note that this version makes no use of analyticity.

== Proof of the real version ==

A simple proof is as follows.

:<math>
\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \int_a^b \frac{f(x)}{x\pm i \varepsilon}\,dx = \mp i \pi \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \int_a^b \frac{\varepsilon}{\pi(x^2+\varepsilon^2)}f(x)\,dx + \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \int_a^b \frac{x^2}{x^2+\varepsilon^2} \, \frac{f(x)}{x}\, dx.</math>

For the first term, <math>\frac{\varepsilon}{\pi(x^2 + \varepsilon^2)} </math> is a [[nascent delta function]], and therefore approaches a [[Dirac delta function]] in the limit. Therefore, the first term equals <math> \mp i \pi f(0) </math>.

For the second term, the factor <math>\frac{x^2}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2} </math> approaches 1 for <math> |x| \gg \varepsilon </math>, approaches 0 for <math> |x| \ll \varepsilon </math>, and is exactly symmetric about 0. Therefore, in the limit, it turns the integral into a [[Cauchy principal value]] integral.

== Physics application ==

In [[quantum mechanics]] and [[quantum field theory]], one often has to evaluate integrals of the form

:<math>\int_{-\infty}^\infty dE\, \int_0^\infty dt\, f(E)\exp(-iEt)</math>

where ''E'' is some energy and ''t'' is time. This expression, as written, is undefined (since the time integral does not converge), so it is typically modified by adding a negative real term to ''-iEt'' in the exponential, and then taking that to zero, i.e.:

:<math>\begin{align} & \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \int_{-\infty}^\infty dE\, \int_0^\infty dt\, f(E)\exp(-iEt-\varepsilon t )= \\ & -i \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0^+} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{f(E)}{E-i\varepsilon}\,dE  = \pi f(0)-i \mathcal{P}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f(E)}{E}\,dE,\end{align}</math>

where the latter step uses the real version of the theorem.

=== Heitler function ===
In [[Quantum optics|theoretical quantum optics]], the derivation of a [[Lindbladian|master equation in Lindblad form]] often requires the following integral function,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Breuer |first=Heinz-Peter |title=The Theory of Open Quantum Systems |last2=Petruccione |first2=Francesco |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-19-852063-4 |pages=145 |language=en |doi=10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199213900.001.0001}}</ref> which is a direct consequence of the Sokhotski–Plemelj theorem and is often called the '''Heitler-function''':
:<math> \int_0^\infty d\tau\, \exp(-i(\omega \pm \nu)\tau) = \pi \delta(\omega \pm \nu) - i \mathcal{P} \Big(\frac{1}{\omega \pm \nu}\Big)</math>
